content.text: Two Claude Code sessions have separate conversations, but in one checkout they share everything on disk: the files, the branch, the git index and whatever the tests run against. Give each parallel session its own git worktree with
, so each one edits its own copy on its own branch, and merge the branches when they're done.

You open two terminals in the same repo. In the first, Claude adds rate limiting to the API middleware. In the second, Claude fixes a flaky date test. Twenty minutes in, the test session runs the whole suite, sees three middleware tests failing because the first session is halfway through its change, and "fixes" them by putting the old middleware code back. Then the first session commits with
, and the date-test fix ships inside a commit titled "Add rate limiting". Nothing crashed. Each session did something reasonable with the files it saw.
"Each Claude Code session is independent, so I can run several in the same checkout and their edits won't collide." There's a lot of truth in the first half:

items.text: Each session has its own conversation and context window; one never sees the other's chat.
Claude reads files fresh on each tool call, so a session picks up the other one's edits the next time it reads.
Claude's Edit tool matches against the file's current content, so two sessions rarely garble the same line.
When the tasks touch different files, it often works fine for a while.

content.text: The half-truth: the conversations are isolated, the working directory isn't. Both sessions act on one set of files, one branch and one staging area, and each makes decisions from a state the other is changing.
One checkout is one shared state
A checkout is more than files. It has one
, so one branch checked out at a time, and one index, the staging area your next commit comes from. Two sessions in it share all of that:

items.text: Half-finished work is visible.
Tests, builds and linters run against both sessions' edits at once, so a failure can belong to the other task, and a session that "fixes" it may undo the other's work in progress.
Git operations are global.
git checkout
git stash
or
git reset
in one session changes the files under the other.
git add -A
in one sweeps the other's edits into its commit.
Undo doesn't know about the other session.
Checkpoints
track files edited in the current session, and "edits from other concurrent sessions are normally not captured, unless they happen to modify the same files as the current session".

content.text: What a worktree gives each session

is, in the docs' words, "a separate working directory with its own files and branch, sharing the same repository history and remote as your main checkout". Git's own docs add that a linked worktree shares everything "except per-worktree files such as HEAD, index, etc.", so each one gets its own branch and staging area.

, branched from your default branch, and starts the session there. While a session is isolated, Claude Code blocks its edits to paths in the main checkout, commands whose working directory resolves there, and git redirected into it with

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Terminal 1
cd ~/src/shop && claude
# Terminal 2: same files, same branch, same index
cd ~/src/shop && claude

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Terminal 1: .claude/worktrees/rate-limit, branch worktree-rate-limit
cd ~/src/shop && claude --worktree rate-limit
# Terminal 2: its own copy of the files on its own branch
cd ~/src/shop && claude --worktree flaky-date-test

content.text: With worktrees, the story plays out differently. The test session runs the suite against its own copy, where the middleware is untouched, so the only failure it sees is its own. Each session commits to its own branch, and you decide how the two branches come together.

The isolation also has edges. The docs scope worktrees to isolating "file edits", so anything outside the files is still shared: two dev servers on the same port or two test runs against one local database still collide. And the isolation checks read paths and command text, so a command that writes into the main checkout without running git there, such as
or a shell redirect, isn't refused by them.
